questions.question: A model must fill a missing word using words both before and after the gap. Which training setup matches BERT?
options: Speaker identity classification
Causal next-token prediction
Bidirectional masked language modeling
Audio-to-text sequence transduction
questions.explanation: BERT trains an encoder to recover selected missing tokens from context on both the left and right, so it fits a gap whose answer depends on following words. Causal next-token prediction hides that future context by design.

questions.question: Of 100 tokens selected for BERT’s masking objective, how many are replaced with [MASK] under the 80/10/10 rule?
options: 10 tokens
15 tokens
90 tokens
80 tokens
questions.explanation: The 80/10/10 rule is conditioned on the 100 selected positions: 0.80 × 100 = 80 become [MASK]. The separate 15% figure is how many tokens are selected from the full sequence, not the replacement fraction within that subset.

questions.question: Why are some selected tokens replaced with random words or left unchanged?
options: To reduce the train-inference mismatch around [MASK]
To make the encoder attend only to left context
To let the decoder predict the following sentence
To reserve [MASK] for the classification head
questions.explanation: Only using [MASK] would expose the model to a marker absent at inference, creating a train-inference distribution shift. Random replacements and unchanged selected tokens vary the input; they do not make the encoder left-context-only.

questions.question: A selected token is left unchanged by the 10% rule. Which label should the MLM objective use there?
options: The unchanged input is relabeled as [MASK]
The next token becomes the prediction target
Its original token ID remains the prediction target
The ignore index replaces the original target
questions.explanation: Even when the input is left unchanged, the selected position still has a training target: its original token ID. The ignore index is assigned to unselected positions, so using it here would remove a required prediction loss.

questions.question: A product needs sentiment classification and semantic retrieval embeddings. Which model direction does the lesson recommend?
options: A waveform tokenizer with a causal audio decoder
An encoder-decoder model for every query
A decoder-only model that generates full answers
An encoder-only model such as BERT
questions.explanation: Encoder-only models provide bidirectional representations efficiently for classification and retrieval, the two needs named here. A decoder generating full answers adds an autoregressive objective and is unnecessary for these embedding and label tasks.

questions.question: A downstream task labels each token in a sentence, such as named-entity recognition. What encoder property is useful?
options: Causal masking with one final output state
A whole-sequence label with no token states
Bidirectional context with per-position outputs
A decoder cross-attending to a separate source
questions.explanation: NER needs a contextual representation at every token so each position can receive its own label. A whole-sequence label discards token locations, while the encoder’s bidirectional per-position states preserve them.
